verses.translation_literal: Sing to YHWH a new song; sing to YHWH, all the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: Sing! Lift your voice to the LORD, and let the song be one nobody has sung before. Sing to the LORD, all the earth, every tongue under the sky.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens with an order, and the order is shouted, not coaxed: the imperative 'sing' is plural, and it comes three times in the first two verses. Play it as a crowd being called into the street, not a choir warming up. 'All the earth' is the whole inhabited world, not just Israel, and the listener must feel how large that is for a small nation under imperial thumbs. Ancient singers knew a set repertoire of temple songs; a 'new song' is a song made for something the LORD has just done, and the Bible keeps the phrase for rescue and victory (Ps 33:3, 98:1, Isa 42:10). The traditional commentators disagree about when: Rashi says always 'for the future', Radak hears the return from Babylon. Ask the actors to choose what has just happened.

The KJV 'O sing unto the Lord' is accurate but its 'O' and 'unto' make the line sound like a hymnbook. The Hebrew is a stamping, repeating sound: shiru ... shir ... shiru. The root appears three times in eight words (the verb twice and the noun once), and the English should repeat it.

philological_notes.note: 'A new song': the noun and the verb come from one root, so the line sings the word it commands. 'New' marks a song made for a fresh act of the LORD, not one merely never heard.
'All the earth' can mean 'all the land' or 'all the inhabitants of the earth'. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri take it as the people living on it, as in Gen 41:57, where 'all the earth' came to Egypt.

verses.translation_literal: Sing to YHWH, bless his name; bear news from day to day of his salvation.
verses.translation_dramatic: Sing to the LORD. Bless his name. And do not let a day go by without carrying the news from one to the next: he has saved.
verses.directors_commentary:
The command to sing now becomes a command to bless and then to carry news. The verb basar is the verb of the runner who comes in from the battlefield: a messenger arrives breathless, and what he carries is good. It is not a word for 'show forth', as the KJV has it, which sounds like a display in a shop window. Someone is out of breath with it. Radak notes that news is sweet when heard fresh, and that we should tell the story of salvation 'as though it happened today'. Tell the actors that every day is a first telling.

'Salvation' (yeshu'ah) is concrete in the ancient world: it means to be brought out of a tight place, from siege, famine or enemies, into open space. 'Bless his name' has an unusual object: usually a person blesses a person; here the name stands in for the LORD himself, as in the rest of the psalm.

philological_notes.note: The root means to bring news, normally good news such as a victory or a birth. Metzudat Zion defines it simply as 'making new things heard', and Radak stresses that its sweetness lies in its newness.
'His salvation': rescue into space and safety. The word is the same root as the names Joshua and Jesus (Yeshua).

verses.translation_literal: Recount among the nations his glory, among all the peoples his wonders.
verses.translation_dramatic: Tell it to the nations: the glory of the LORD. Tell it to every people: the wonders he has done.
verses.directors_commentary:
The news now crosses a border. The audience is no longer fellow Israelites but 'the nations', the goyim, a word that to a Judean ear meant the neighbours and the empires, often hostile. KJV 'heathen' is the weak point here: it turns an ethnic and political term (nations) into a religious insult and loses the point that they are being addressed as peoples, not as pagans. Ibn Ezra notes that mentioning the nations makes 'all the earth' in verse 1 mean the land of Israel. Radak adds the political sting: the glory is what the LORD did for you before the eyes of nations that despised you. Play the line as mission and also as defiance.

The verb sapar is 'to count' and so 'to recount': the story is told like a ledger, item by item. 'Wonders' (nifla'ot) are acts that exceed human power; they are what the Exodus tradition calls the LORD's signature (Ex 3:20).

philological_notes.note: From the root 'to count', so 'to recount' in order, with the same consonants as 'book' (sefer) and 'scribe'. The piel gives it the force of a full telling.
'His wonders': things too extraordinary for human hands, used above all for the LORD's acts in the Exodus.

verses.translation_literal: For great is YHWH and to be praised exceedingly; to be feared is he above all gods.
verses.translation_dramatic: For great is the LORD, and worthy of praise beyond measure. He is the one to be feared, high above every god the nations have named.
verses.directors_commentary:
The 'for' (ki) gives the reason for the command: the reason to sing, bless and tell is who he is. The sentence has two passive participles in a row, 'to be praised' and 'to be feared', which say not 'he is praised' but 'he deserves it'. Notice the fear: nora' is the word for awe that makes the knees weak, not courtesy. The KJV 'greatly to be praised' is fine, and its 'he is to be feared above all gods' is accurate, but readers hear 'above' as a ranking among equals, and the next verse takes that away.

The phrase 'above all gods' is where the psalm picks its fight. In the ancient Near East, every nation had its gods, and rivalry among them was the normal way to speak of power. The psalmist uses the vocabulary of that rivalry in order to cancel it. Ibn Ezra and Radak read 'elohim' as angels; Metzudat David as the sun, moon and stars worshipped by idolaters. Since verse 5 will call the gods of the nations nothing at all, the reading as foreign gods is the natural one.

philological_notes.note: A plural form that can mean 'gods', 'God' or 'divine beings'. Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as angels; Metzudat David as the heavenly bodies that were worshipped. Here it is set against 'the gods of the peoples' in the next verse.
A niphal participle of 'to fear': 'one to be feared', that is, awe-inspiring. It is the same root as the verb for 'fear of the LORD'.

verses.translation_literal: For all the gods of the peoples are 'elilim, and YHWH made the heavens.
verses.translation_dramatic: For all the gods of the peoples are nothing: hollow things, idols. But the LORD, the LORD made the heavens.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the sharpest line of the psalm, and it rests on a sound. The Hebrew word for 'gods' is 'elohim; the word for 'idols' is 'elilim, which sounds almost the same, a few letters different, with the effect of 'gods? good-for-nothings.' The English cannot reproduce it easily, so the dramatic layer lets the voice drop from one word to the next. Metzudat Zion and Ibn Ezra hear in it 'el' plus 'lo' (no god), 'something that is not' (compare 'physicians of nothing', Job 13:4, in their citation); that is an old folk etymology, and it expresses the force even if modern lexicons are cautious about it.

The KJV 'idols' is correct but flat, and the YLT 'nought' catches the sense better. The contrast is concrete: foreign gods are things people carve and carry; the LORD is the one who made the heavens, where the nations located their gods. For the sun, moon and stars were gods in Egypt and Mesopotamia. Radak and Meiri read the 'gods' as precisely these heavenly bodies, now demoted to creatures. The last clause begins with the LORD's name and puts the object, the heavens, before the verb, which stresses the contrast: gods of the peoples, nothing; but YHWH, the heavens he made.

philological_notes.note: A contemptuous plural, 'worthless things' and later 'idols'. It echoes 'elohim' in sound. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion connect it to 'not / nothing', as in 'physicians of nothing' (Job 13:4); that derivation is traditional and disputed.
The word order puts 'heavens' before the verb, for emphasis: the realm where the nations placed their gods is the LORD's own handiwork.

verses.translation_literal: Splendor and majesty are before him; strength and beauty are in his sanctuary.
verses.translation_dramatic: Splendor and majesty go before him like heralds. Strength and beauty fill his sanctuary.
verses.directors_commentary:
Four abstract nouns stand in two pairs, like four attendants flanking a throne: hod and hadar, 'oz and tif'eret. The ancient reader would picture them as an entourage, almost persons, as Ps 85:14 sends righteousness before him. 'Before him' (lefanav) means 'in his face, in his presence', the place where courtiers stand. The KJV 'honour and majesty' and 'strength and beauty' are fine words but are quietly Victorian: 'honour' is for a gentleman, while hod is the glow of royalty, a word used for the king's own splendor (Ps 21:6).

The 'sanctuary' (miqdash) is where the psalm points the listener, from the nations out in the world back to a place. Ibn Ezra and Radak think the heavens, with Ibn Ezra preferring the Temple and the ark, 'the strength' (cf. Ps 78:61). The strongest reading for a performance is the Temple: a procession ends at a courtyard in the next verses. Malbim distinguishes the inner nature (hod, 'oz) from the outward show (hadar, tif'eret), which a director can use: the first pair is what he is, the second what shows.

philological_notes.note: A fixed pair for royal splendor. Malbim distinguishes hod as inward and hadar as the outward beauty seen by the eyes.
'Strength and beauty'. Ibn Ezra points out that 'oz is also the name given to the ark (Ps 78:61, 132:8), which he thinks is meant here.
'His sanctuary', a holy place. Whether it is the Temple or the heavens is disputed by Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri.

verses.translation_literal: Ascribe to YHWH, families of peoples, ascribe to YHWH glory and strength.
verses.translation_dramatic: Give to the LORD, you families of the nations, give to the LORD: glory and strength.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first command in the psalm addressed to the nations by name. 'Families of peoples' (mishpechot 'amim) is a warm phrase: it speaks of kin groups, clans, not armies, the way Genesis 10 lists the 'families of the sons of Noah'. The psalm turns the listeners from messengers into members of one family tree, all invited. The verb hav is a short, almost abrupt word, 'give!' or 'bring!', which the KJV renders 'give', as does BBE; 'ascribe' (YLT, ASV) is more exact, because what is given is not a gift in the hand but a recognition in speech: say that glory and strength are his. Rashi puts the question and answer plainly, 'What shall you give him? Glory and strength', and Ibn Ezra insists it is done 'in the mouth'.

What the verse imitates is the language of the tribute: vassals give their overlord honour and strength. In the surrounding world that is what a conquered king did when he handed over goods. Here the tribute is to the LORD and it is voluntary. The doubled 'give to the LORD' is rhythmic, like a drumbeat leading the procession in.

philological_notes.note: An imperative of the rare root 'to give', used in commands and calls ('come, let us...'). Metzudat Zion glosses it simply 'give', and says it means to give in speech (compare Job 1:22).
'Families of peoples': clans, as in the table of nations in Gen 10. KJV 'kindreds of the people' keeps the kinship sense.

verses.translation_literal: Ascribe to YHWH the glory of his name; lift up an offering and come to his courts.
verses.translation_dramatic: Give to the LORD the glory his name deserves. Lift up your offering, and come into his courts.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speech becomes a procession. Words give way to the body: 'lift up' (se'u), 'come' (bo'u). A minchah is a gift brought to a superior, whether grain offered at the altar or tribute brought to a king; Metzudat David pictures it literally carried on the shoulder, which is what the Hebrew verb 'lift' implies. The 'courts' (chatzerot) are the open enclosures around the sanctuary, where a worshipper may stand; the inner house is for priests. The KJV 'the glory due unto his name' is a fair rendering of the genitive 'glory of his name' (Metzudat David: 'the glory fitting for his name'); the Hebrew itself is only 'glory of his name', and the 'due' is supplied.

BBE changes 'courts' to 'his house' and so loses the picture of a crowd standing in an open yard. The actors should imagine people who are not allowed in the room but are admitted to the forecourt. Ibn Ezra reads 'name' as the ark, called by the Name; the plain sense is that the name stands for the LORD himself, as in verse 2.

philological_notes.note: A gift to a superior: a cereal offering in the temple, or tribute to a king. Here it is carried ('lift up') into the courts.
'His courts': the enclosures of the sanctuary, where a lay person could enter. Radak says these are the courts of the Temple.

verses.translation_literal: Bow down to YHWH in the splendor of holiness; writhe from before him, all the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: Bow down before the LORD in the splendor of holiness. Tremble before his face, all the earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The crowd has reached the courts, and the body goes down. 'Bow down' (hishtachavu) is the full prostration, the way one approaches a king: the face to the ground. The line then does something that polite English hides: chilu is a verb for shaking and also for the pains of childbirth, so 'tremble' is the soft word for what the Hebrew pictures as a convulsion. Radak says that the earth had not trembled before, and now, seeing his wonders, it does. The KJV 'fear before him' strips that physical shake away.

The phrase hadrat-qodesh is notoriously ambiguous. The KJV has 'the beauty of holiness' (hence the old hymn), the ASV 'in holy array', the BBE 'in holy robes'. The Hebrew can mean either the splendor which holiness gives, the holy attire the worshipper wears, or the holy appearance of God. The literal layer keeps all three open. For a director: the whole earth is in its best clothes and on its knees, shaking. Radak and Metzudat David say it is the Temple, 'made splendid with holiness'; Ibn Ezra, that the bowing is done while bringing the offering, 'in trembling and fear'.

philological_notes.note: 'In the splendor / adornment of holiness'. The sense could be holy attire (ASV, BBE), the holy place (Radak, Metzudat David) or the splendor of holiness itself (KJV). The same phrase appears in Ps 29:2 and 1 Chr 16:29.
'Writhe, tremble': the root also describes the pangs of childbirth and the shaking of the earth. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'trembling and quaking'.

verses.translation_literal: Say among the nations: YHWH reigns! Indeed the world is established, it will not be shaken; he will judge peoples with uprightness.
verses.translation_dramatic: Say it among the nations: the LORD reigns! The world stands firm; it will not be shaken. He will judge the peoples, and judge them straight.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the heart of the psalm and its cry: yhwh malak. The short formula has two senses and the first is nearer a coronation shout, like 'the king is dead, long live the king': it announces an enthronement, which is why some translate 'the LORD has become king' (YLT 'hath reigned'). Others, the KJV and ASV, 'reigneth', treat it as a standing fact. A director can play it as a news bulletin and as a trumpet blast. The cry is to be spread to the nations, completing the movement from verse 3.

The second clause answers a fear. In the ancient world, the order of things (the earth, the seasons, the borders) was held against chaos by the gods and was always in danger. The statement that the world 'will not be shaken' (bal-timmot) says that this order is anchored in his rule, and not in rival powers. 'Tevel' is the inhabited, fertile world, not the bare earth.

'He will judge the peoples with uprightness' sounds comfortable in English, where judging means condemning. In Hebrew, to judge (din) is to govern, to set things right, to defend the wronged, so this is good news for the oppressed. Meishar means a level road: a straight, even path. The KJV 'righteously' is acceptable, but the picture is of a straight road, in which the courts do not twist. Rashi relates it to the days when the nations will be given a pure language (Zeph 3:9); Radak to the justice he did in the nations who came against Jerusalem.

philological_notes.note: A formula of enthronement, as in Ps 93:1, 97:1 and 99:1. The perfect verb can mean 'has become king' or 'reigns'. The accent shows that it forms a clause of its own, the content of what is to be said among the nations.
The inhabited world, the productive earth, a poetic word used in parallel with 'earth' and 'world'.
'With uprightness, evenness'. The root means straight, level. Rashi glosses it as 'merits' or 'good deeds'; Metzudat David as judgment according to mercy.

verses.translation_literal: Let the heavens rejoice and let the earth exult; let the sea thunder, and its fullness.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth be glad. Let the sea thunder, and everything that fills it.
verses.directors_commentary:
The audience widens from the nations to the cosmos. The two verbs of joy are different: simchah (rejoice) is the steady joy; gil (be glad, exult) is the leap and the spin. Malbim builds on that difference, but the point for an actor is simpler: the heavens smile and the earth dances. Then the sea. The Hebrew verb is ra'am, 'to thunder', the sound of storm and thunderclap, and the KJV 'roar' is too tame and too animal. In the Canaanite stories the sea was an enemy of the gods; here it thunders in applause, a chaos power now giving a cheer for its king. The 'fullness' of the sea means everything in it, the fish and creatures (Radak, Metzudat David).

This verse is no metaphor to the ancients but a picture of the world as a crowd. Metzudat David and Radak call it a figure of speech for a great joy, and say that on a day of evil, the sun and moon darken (Joel 2:10): creation reacts. A director might give the sea the loudest part.

philological_notes.note: 'Let it thunder': the verb used of the thunder and of the sea's roar. Rashi glosses it as raising the voice in praise; Metzudat David as making a loud sound for great joy.
To exult or spin with joy. Malbim distinguishes gil, joy at something new, from simchah, steady joy.
'And its fullness': what fills the sea. Radak says the fish; Metzudat David, the creatures that fill it.

verses.translation_literal: Let exult [the] field, and all that [is] in it; then they will sing out, all [the] trees of [the] forest.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let the open field exult, and everything that lives within it. And then, from the far dark edge of the woods, the voice of the forest breaks: every tree there ringing out in song.
verses.directors_commentary:
Heaven and earth and sea have already been called to joy (verse 11); now the call drops down to dry land, to the cultivated field and the wild forest. Play it as a descent in scale, from the vast to the near, and from the open to the shaded. The field is where an Israelite's life is decided: rain or drought, harvest or hunger. The forest is the opposite, uncultivated and uncounted. The psalm gathers both, the tamed and the wild, into one chorus.

The Hebrew sets the two halves in sequence with a small word, 'az, 'then': first the field exults, and only then do the trees sing. 'Exult' (ya'aloz) is a word of physical, leaping gladness; 'sing out' (yeranenu) is the ringing cry of a crowd, the same root as the shout of the temple liturgy. The KJV's 'rejoice' flattens both verbs into one tame word, and 'wood' is an old-fashioned singular for what the Hebrew calls ya'ar, the forest. The Hebrew sentence does not end here: the phrase 'before YHWH' (lifnei YHWH) belongs to the next verse, where it opens the reason for all this joy ('for he comes'). Webster's rendering, not the KJV's, carries 'before the LORD' back into this verse; the Hebrew verse itself stops at 'trees of the forest', so the trees sing, and the reader waits a beat to learn before whom.

Trees singing is not a stretch for the original audience; creation praising its maker is standard psalm language, and in a land of scattered woods and terraced hills the forest was a place of mystery. Medieval readers took the trees as a figure: Rashi on Psalm 96:12 reads 'all the trees of the forest' as 'all the rulers of the nations'. Meiri takes the verse as a picture of great peace and abundance, the reverse of the withered earth in Isaiah 24:4.

philological_notes.note: To exult, to leap with joy; a strong word for visible, bodily gladness rather than quiet contentment. The form is an unmarked imperfect that English can read as a wish ('let it exult') or a statement. Metzudat Zion glosses it simply as 'to be glad'.

A poetic form of the word for field (sadeh), here the open country as a whole. Radak says it means the field and the wilderness together, and that 'all that is in it' means the wild animals; Metzudat David takes it as the creatures found in the field.
To give a ringing cry, to sing out. The verb is intensive (piel) and usually describes a cry of joy raised by many voices together, which is why the singing trees are a choir and not a solo.

verses.translation_literal: Before YHWH, for he has come, for he has come to judge the earth; he will judge [the] world in righteousness, and peoples in his faithfulness.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let it all be done before the LORD, for he is coming. He is coming! He comes to judge the earth. He will judge the whole world with justice, and every people with a faithfulness that does not waver.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the last line of the psalm, and the whole poem has been building to it. The sea roars, the fields exult, the trees of the forest sing, and the reason for the noise is given at the end: the king is arriving. The verse opens with a bare 'before YHWH', a fragment with no verb, as if the singers have stopped and are standing in the presence they were praising. Then comes 'for he has come' twice, which is not filler. Radak says the second clause explains the first and that the doubling adds strength. Malbim reads it as two arrivals. The KJV makes both 'cometh', but the Hebrew verb is a perfect, a completed form, so a singer is announcing a coming already under way, the way a watchman says 'he's here' when the dust cloud is still on the road. Actors should play it as breathless certainty, not as a prediction.

The word 'judge' (shaphat) needs a modern correction. In the ancient Near East a king was first of all the judge: he heard the case of the widow, overturned the thief's gain and set the land right. To 'judge the earth' is therefore good news, which is why the trees are singing. It is not a threat, and it does not mean a courtroom of condemnation. The KJV's 'judge the earth' and 'judge the world' are accurate, but the English word has lost this sense of setting things right. The Hebrew sets two nouns side by side: 'earth' ('eretz) and 'world' (tevel), the inhabited, fertile land. The KJV renders 'in righteousness' as 'with righteousness', which is looser, since the Hebrew preposition be- gives the sphere or manner in which he judges, as a judge acts 'in' justice and not 'with' it as an instrument. At the verse's end the KJV 'his truth' is the one real softening. 'Emunah' is faithfulness, the steadiness of something you can lean your weight on, and 'truth' makes it sound like a doctrine. YLT and BBE ('faithfulness', 'unchanging faith') are closer. The tone is pointed against the gods of the neighbours. Their rule was seen as arbitrary and capricious. This king is reliable in his judgment. Metzudat David glosses the word as 'truly, as is fitting'.

philological_notes.note: A perfect verb, 'he has come', here said twice. The perfect can show a prophetic certainty, in which the coming is spoken of as done because it is sure. Radak takes the second as an explanation of the first and a strengthening; Malbim distinguishes two comings, one in the natural order and one for judgment.

The same root as 'to judge' earlier in the verse (lishpot), now in the imperfect: he has come to judge, and he will judge. The repetition turns the purpose of the coming into its content. The verb covers the whole work of governing, not only passing sentence.

'In his faithfulness'. The root 'mn means firmness, what bears weight; the noun is reliability, which the KJV's 'truth' hides. The Targum has 'in faithfulness' (בהימנותא) and Metzudat David glosses it 'truly, as is fitting'.
